kernels.name: mul_mat_q (MMQ)

launch_config.global_size_expression: 3D: (1, block_num_y, block_num_x) * (1, nwarps, WARP_SIZE). block_num_x = (ncols_x + mmq_x - 1) / mmq_x, block_num_y = (nrows_x + mmq_y - 1) / mmq_y
launch_config.notes: Work-group size of 64 is well below the recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs. The WARP_SIZE=16 matches native SIMD width, but nwarps=4 gives only 4 sub-groups per work-group. Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] is a correctness risk since the entire kernel assumes WARP_SIZE=16 as the sub-group width.

strided_accesses: X-tile loads have row-stride separation (different rows of the tile separated by blocks_per_row in global memory)
Y-tile loads have per-warp column strides as each warp loads a different column block
memory_patterns.notes: All loads use scalar 4-byte get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned helpers. No sycl::vec or 16-byte loads. Within a sub-group, consecutive lanes read consecutive data from the qs field of quantization blocks, which is reasonably coalesced.

slm_usage.notes: SLM usage is 3-5 KB depending on quantization format, vastly underutilizing the 64 KB available per Xe-core. Bank conflict avoidance uses CUDA-style +1 stride padding (WARP_SIZE+1=17 stride), which may actually cause conflicts on Intel's 16-bank SLM architecture. tile_x_ql, tile_x_dm/tile_x_d, tile_x_sc, tile_x_qh (format-dependent), tile_y_qs, tile_y_ds are allocated.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction needed — each thread accumulates into its own private sum[2][1] and writes a unique output element. This is architecturally correct for the tiling approach.

data_types.notes: Primary compute is integer dot products (dp4a on int8/uint8 quantized values) scaled by float/half factors. Accumulation in float32 is appropriate for numerical stability. joint_matrix could replace dp4a with XMX hardware int8 matmul for significant throughput gains.

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math functions used. All compute is integer bitwise ops, dp4a, and float multiply-add.

hot_loops: Outer K-tiling loop (line 1228): iterates blocks_per_row_x / blocks_per_warp times, NOT unrolled — trip count is data-dependent
qr loop (line 1236): iterates qr times (2 for most formats), UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
Inner k loop (line 1289-1301): iterates WARP_SIZE/(qr*vdr) times (1-2 iterations), NOT unrolled due to register pressure (comment on line 1289)
Inner j loop (line 1291): mmq_x/nwarps = 1 iteration, UNROLLED — trivially 1 iteration
Inner i loop (line 1293): mmq_y/WARP_SIZE = 2 iterations, UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
Load tile loops: 8 iterations each, all UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
loop_analysis.notes: The critical hot inner k-loop is explicitly NOT unrolled due to register pressure (comment says unrolling causes too much register pressure). With the current tiny tile sizes, the inner loop body is only 1-2 iterations. Increasing tile sizes would require revisiting unroll strategy.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: With mmq_x=4 and mmq_y=32, each work-group computes only a 32x4 output tile, resulting in very low arithmetic intensity per memory load. The tiny work-group size (64) also means poor occupancy on Xe2 hardware. The kernel is compute-limited by the lack of XMX utilization — dp4a provides far lower throughput than XMX joint_matrix operations.
anti_patterns: CRITICAL: Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] — kernel assumes WARP_SIZE=16 as sub-group width but doesn't enforce it. Compiler may choose SIMD8 or SIMD32, breaking correctness
CUDA-style SLM bank conflict padding (+1 stride) mismatched for Intel 16-bank SLM
Very small work-group size (64) — well below recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs
Tiny tile sizes (mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32) wasting SLM capacity and limiting compute density
3D nd_range with unused first dimension (always 1) — should be 2D
DPCT migration artifacts: __dpct_inline__, DPCT warning comments, dpct::dp4a calls
CUDA architecture naming (AMPERE, PASCAL, RDNA1/RDNA2) mapped to Intel Gen labels with TODO comments
Manual warp/lane indexing via get_local_id instead of SYCL sub-group APIs
No vectorized memory loads — all scalar 4-byte loads
Massive code duplication: 10 formats x 2 (need_check) = 20 near-identical kernel launches (~1200 lines)

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to the kernel. The entire kernel assumes WARP_SIZE=16 as the sub-group size for indexing, SLM layout, and tile computation. Without this attribute, the compiler may select SIMD8 or SIMD32, potentially breaking correctness. This is a correctness fix first, performance second.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness guarantee. May also improve performance by ensuring the compiler generates SIMD16 code matching the kernel's assumptions. Low single-digit percent speedup from removing compiler ambiguity.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to the lambda in the parallel_for calls (20 launch sites across all formats). Must be placed on the kernel lambda, not a device function.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: This is a correctness fix. Risk is if the kernel actually performs better at a different sub-group size, but the logic requires SIMD16.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase work-group size from 64 to 256 by increasing nwarps from 4 to 16, or by increasing tile dimensions. Current 64-thread work-groups severely underutilize Intel GPU hardware which prefers 256-512. With 64 threads, each Xe-core can run 64/64=1 work-group max per hardware thread slot, leading to poor latency hiding.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% throughput improvement from better occupancy and latency hiding. More sub-groups per work-group means better utilization of the Xe-core's 8 XVEs.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Increase mmq_y to 128 (from 32) and/or mmq_x to 16 (from 4), with nwarps=16. This increases the output tile to 128x16, improving arithmetic intensity. Must also increase SLM allocation proportionally (from ~4KB to ~16-32KB, still well within 64KB limit). Register pressure needs profiling — the inner k-loop unrolling comment may need revisiting.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Larger tiles increase register pressure. The existing comment about unrolling causing register pressure suggests this dimension is sensitive. Needs careful tuning and benchmarking per quantization format.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace scalar dpct::dp4a() calls with joint_matrix (XMX) operations for the integer dot product inner loop. The B60 has 160 XMX engines that provide ~197 Int8 TOPS vs the ~12 TFLOPS of scalar FP32. The inner loop computes int8 dot products that map directly to XMX's int8->int32 matmul capability.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 4-8x throughput improvement for the compute-bound inner loop. XMX provides 16x the peak int8 throughput vs scalar paths, but memory access overhead and tile management limit real-world gains.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Use sycl::ext::oneapi::experimental::matrix::joint_matrix with int8 inputs and int32 accumulator. Requires restructuring the tile loading to match XMX tile sizes (M=8, N=16, K=32 for int8 on Xe2). The quantized data is already in int8 format in SLM, so the primary work is reshaping the data flow. Requires [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] as a prerequisite.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Major kernel rewrite. joint_matrix has strict layout requirements that may not align well with the varied quantization formats (q4_0 through q6_K each have different block structures). May need format-specific XMX tile loaders. Risk of numerical differences in accumulation order.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 16-byte loads (sycl::vec<int,4>) instead of scalar 4-byte loads in the tile loading functions. Adjacent work-items currently each load one 4-byte int; instead, each work-item could load a vec4 (16 bytes), reducing the number of memory transactions by 4x.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-25% improvement in tile loading phase bandwidth utilization. Impact depends on what fraction of kernel time is spent in loads vs compute.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned with reinterpret_cast<sycl::vec<int,4>*> aligned loads where quantization block layout permits. Must ensure 16-byte alignment of source data. The load_tiles_* functions (10 format-specific) each need modification.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment requirements may not always be met depending on quantization block sizes. Some formats (IQ types) have irregular layouts. Need to handle edge cases where the remaining data is less than 16 bytes.

optimization_opportunities.description: Fix SLM bank conflict avoidance for Intel GPU architecture. Current code uses CUDA-style +1 padding (stride WARP_SIZE+1=17) for SLM arrays. Intel SLM has 16 banks with 4-byte granularity. With stride 17, consecutive row accesses hit banks 0,17%16=1,34%16=2,... which is actually conflict-free for row access but may conflict for column access patterns. Analyze actual access patterns and adjust padding for Intel's 16-bank layout.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% improvement in SLM-heavy phases if bank conflicts exist. Requires profiling to quantify actual conflict rate.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace (WARP_SIZE + 1) stride with a stride that avoids conflicts for the actual access patterns in vec_dot_* functions. For Intel's 16 banks, a stride of 17 (WARP_SIZE+1) actually works well for sequential row access but may need adjustment for the interleaved access pattern in the dot product phase. Profile with Intel VTune or Level Zero metrics to measure actual SLM bank conflicts before and after.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: SLM padding changes are localized. Can be benchmarked independently. Low risk of correctness issues.

optimization_opportunities.description: Tune tile configuration per quantization format instead of using one-size-fits-all mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32 for all formats. Different quantization formats have different memory footprints and compute intensities. For example, q4_0 (4-bit, simple) could use larger tiles than q6_K (6-bit, complex scales) without exceeding register or SLM limits.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% improvement for some formats by better matching tile sizes to format complexity.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: The configuration macros already support per-format tile sizes (MMQ_X_Q4_0_AMPERE, etc.). Change the Intel target configuration from the current uniform mmq_x=4, mmq_y=32 to format-specific values. Simpler formats (q4_0, q4_1, q8_0) can use larger tiles; complex formats (q3_K, q5_K, q6_K) may need smaller tiles to avoid register spilling.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires per-format benchmarking. Wrong tile sizes can cause register spilling and severe performance regressions.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace item_ct1.barrier() with item_ct1.barrier(sycl::access::fence_space::local_space) since the barriers only synchronize SLM accesses, not global memory. This tells the hardware that only local memory fence is needed, potentially reducing barrier overhead.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-3% improvement. Barriers are executed twice per qr iteration, so the effect compounds but is still minor.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change the two barrier() calls in the mul_mat_q template (lines ~1287 and ~1312) to barrier(sycl::access::fence_space::local_space). Verify that no global memory synchronization is actually needed between the barrier points.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: If any global memory accesses actually depend on the barrier (e.g., the output write at the end), this would be incorrect. Analysis shows the barriers are only for SLM coherence, so local_space fence should suffice.

optimization_opportunities.description: Investigate whether the hot inner k-loop (line ~1289) can be partially unrolled now that the target is Intel GPU (different register file characteristics than NVIDIA). The comment says unrolling causes too much register pressure, but this was likely profiled on NVIDIA hardware. Intel Xe2 has 512 bytes GRF per thread in SIMD16 mode.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% if register pressure permits. The k-loop has only 1-2 iterations for most formats, so full unroll would eliminate the loop overhead entirely.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Try adding #pragma unroll to the k-loop for simple formats (q4_0, q8_0) first. Monitor register usage via -cl-intel-greater-than-4GB-buffer-required or IGC internal flags. If registers spill, revert.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Register spilling on Intel GPUs causes performance cliffs (spill to SLM or global memory). Must benchmark each format individually.

kernels.efficiency_notes: This is a DPCT-migrated kernel running with CUDA-optimized tile sizes (optimized for NVIDIA Ampere with warp size 32, then scaled down to warp size 16). The work-group size of 64 is far below Intel's preferred 256-512. No XMX utilization despite having 160 XMX engines. Scalar dp4a instead of hardware matrix multiply. Minimal SLM utilization (3-5 KB of 64 KB available). No vectorized loads. The kernel functions correctly but is leaving substantial performance on the table.

kernels.name: mul_mat_vec_q (MMVQ)

launch_config.global_size_expression: Legacy: (1, 1, ceil(nrows/MMV_Y)) * (1, 1, WARP_SIZE). Reordered: (1, 1, block_num_y * WARP_SIZE) with WG=(1, 1, num_subgroups*WARP_SIZE)
launch_config.notes: Two distinct launch patterns: legacy kernels (used for 17 of 20 formats) have a work-group size of only 16 (1 sub-group), which is far below Intel's recommended 256-512. Reordered kernels (Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K only) use 256 work-items (16 sub-groups per work-group), which is properly tuned. GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y=1 means only 1 row per sub-group. All launches correctly specify [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]].

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Legacy kernels use AoS (array-of-structures) block layout where adjacent sub-group lanes read different offsets within the same quantization block — not truly coalesced across blocks. Reordered kernels use SoA (structure-of-arrays) layout with contiguous quants separated from scales, providing much better coalescing.
strided_accesses: Legacy: x[ibx] indexed by row*blocks_per_row + i — AoS layout means quantization block fields (qs, d, qh, sc) are interleaved, causing strided access to each field
Legacy: y[iby] indexed similarly with interleaved q8_1 block fields
memory_patterns.notes: All loads use scalar 4-byte helpers: get_int_from_uint8() reconstructs ints from bytes, get_int_from_int8_aligned() does direct 4-byte cast. No sycl::vec types for memory loads. The reordered kernels access contiguous quant/scale regions via separated pointers, which is more bandwidth-efficient.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM (shared local memory) is used by any MMVQ kernel variant. All communication is done via sub-group shuffles (dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor in legacy, sycl::reduce_over_group in reordered). This means the Y vector data — shared across all sub-groups in a work-group — is redundantly loaded from global memory by each sub-group in the reordered kernels.

reduction_pattern.reduction_details: Legacy: manual butterfly reduction via dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor (DPCT artifact of CUDA __shfl_xor_sync), #pragma unroll for log2(WARP_SIZE)=4 iterations. Reordered: proper sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, val, std::plus<>()). Each sub-group reduces its partial dot product to a single scalar for one output row.

data_types.notes: FP32 accumulation is appropriate for numerical stability. Integer dp4a for quantized dot products. Optional GGML_SYCL_F16 build flag enables half-precision scale arithmetic in some vec_dot functions. joint_matrix is not directly applicable to matrix-vector (single vector) but could be used if multiple vectors were batched.

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math functions. All compute is integer bitwise ops, dp4a, and float multiply-add.

hot_loops: Main block loop (line ~80): iterates blocks_per_row/blocks_per_warp times, NOT unrolled (dynamic trip count based on ncols)
Inner elem loop (line ~84): iterates qi/vdr/WARP_SIZE times — typically 0 or 1 iterations for most formats, NOT unrolled in legacy (but IS unrolled in reordered kernels)
Reduction loop (line ~93): log2(WARP_SIZE)=4 iterations, UNROLLED via #pragma unroll
vecdotq.hpp inner loops: all short constant-trip-count loops with #pragma unroll (e.g., QR2_K=4, QR4_K=2 iterations)
loop_analysis.notes: Inner loops in vecdotq.hpp are properly unrolled. The main block loop cannot be unrolled (dynamic). The reordered kernels are better optimized with #pragma unroll on the inner element loop.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Matrix-vector multiplication is inherently memory-bandwidth bound: each weight element is loaded once and used for exactly one multiply-add (arithmetic intensity ~0.5 ops/byte for Q4 formats). The B60's compute intensity threshold is ~27 ops/byte, so MMVQ is far below — it needs maximum memory bandwidth utilization. The legacy kernel's 16-thread work-group and AoS layout hurt bandwidth efficiency.
anti_patterns: Legacy kernels: work-group size of 16 (1 sub-group) — far below Intel's recommended 256-512, poor occupancy and latency hiding
Legacy kernels: manual butterfly shuffle reduction (dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor) instead of sycl::reduce_over_group — DPCT artifact
DPCT artifacts throughout: dpct::dp4a, dpct::vectorized_binary, dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor, __dpct_inline__, DPCT_COMPATIBILITY_TEMP guards
3D nd_range with 2 unused dimensions (both dim0 and dim1 are trivially 1) — should be 1D
No SLM caching of Y vector — in reordered kernels with 16 sub-groups, each sub-group redundantly loads the same Y data from global memory (16x bandwidth waste for Y)
No vectorized loads — all scalar 4-byte loads via get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned
Reorder support limited to 3 of 20 quantization formats (Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K) — other formats stuck with legacy AoS layout
Massive code duplication: 10 IQ-specific kernel functions nearly identical to the generic mul_mat_vec_q template (~430 lines of duplicate code)
~20 nearly-identical launcher functions differing only in template parameters (~500 lines)

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase legacy kernel work-group size from 16 to 256 by adopting the reordered kernel's multi-sub-group pattern (16 sub-groups per work-group). Currently 17 of 20 formats use the legacy launch with only 16 work-items per work-group, resulting in severely underutilized Intel GPU hardware. Each sub-group still computes one row independently, but grouping 16 sub-groups into one work-group enables better scheduling and occupancy.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 25-50% throughput improvement from better occupancy and memory-level parallelism. This is the single highest-impact optimization for MMVQ on Intel GPUs. The reordered kernel paths already demonstrate this pattern works correctly.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change the legacy launcher from block_dims=(1,1,WARP_SIZE) to block_dims=(1,1,num_subgroups*WARP_SIZE) with num_subgroups=16. Adjust block_nums accordingly: block_num_z = ceil(nrows / (GGML_SYCL_MMV_Y * num_subgroups)). Each sub-group uses its sub-group ID to compute a different row. The reordered kernels (lines 537-554) serve as the template.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The reordered kernels already prove this pattern works for Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K. The same pattern is straightforward to apply to all other formats since sub-groups are independent. Only risk is if nrows is not a multiple of 16 — need bounds checking (already present in the kernel via row < nrows guard).

optimization_opportunities.description: Cache Y vector data in SLM for the multi-sub-group work-groups. In the reordered kernels (and the proposed multi-sub-group legacy kernels), all 16 sub-groups in a work-group iterate over the same Y vector. Currently each sub-group independently loads Y from global memory, wasting 16x bandwidth on Y. By loading Y once per work-group into SLM and sharing it, Y-related global memory traffic drops by ~16x.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-30% overall throughput improvement for memory-bound MMVQ. Y vector is typically ncols/QK8_1 blocks of 36 bytes each. For a 4096-column matrix with Q4_0: ncols/32 * 36 = 4608 bytes — easily fits in the 64KB SLM budget.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Allocate sycl::local_accessor for Y data. Have sub-group 0 (or all sub-groups cooperatively) load Y into SLM. Insert group_barrier(). Then all sub-groups read Y from SLM instead of global memory. For the main loop, load the next tile of Y data in a double-buffered fashion to overlap global loads with SLM reads.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Adds SLM pressure and barriers. For very large ncols, Y may not fit in SLM entirely — need tiled loading. The barrier overhead must not exceed the bandwidth savings. For small nrows (few sub-groups active), the benefit diminishes.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace all 10 instances of manual dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor butterfly reduction in legacy kernels with sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, val, sycl::plus<float>()). The reordered kernels already use the correct SYCL idiom. The manual shuffle reduction is a DPCT artifact and may not compile to optimal code on Intel GPUs.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 3-8% improvement. The compiler may generate better reduction code from the high-level reduce_over_group API than from the manual butterfly pattern. More importantly, it removes a DPCT dependency.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In each of the 10 IQ-variant kernels and the generic mul_mat_vec_q, replace the '#pragma unroll for (mask = WARP_SIZE/2; ...) { tmp += dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor(sg, tmp, mask); }' with 'tmp = sycl::reduce_over_group(item_ct1.get_sub_group(), tmp, sycl::plus<float>());'. Alternatively, use the existing warp_reduce_sum() helper from common.hpp.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Direct replacement with standard SYCL API. The reordered kernels already prove this works correctly. No algorithmic change — same mathematical result.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 8-byte or 16-byte loads (sycl::vec<uint32_t, 2> or sycl::vec<uint32_t, 4>) for loading quantization blocks from global memory. Currently all loads are scalar 4-byte via get_int_from_uint8/get_int_from_int8_aligned. Wider loads reduce the number of memory transactions and better utilize the memory bus.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% improvement in memory throughput for the weight loading phase. Impact is higher for simpler formats (Q4_0, Q8_0) where the quant data is more regular.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In vecdotq.hpp vec_dot functions, replace pairs of sequential get_int calls with a single sycl::vec<uint32_t, 2> load. For Q4_0: currently loads v.x and v.y separately — load as sycl::vec<uint32_t, 2>. Must verify 8-byte alignment of quantization block qs fields. The reordered layout (contiguous quants) is more amenable to vectorization than the AoS layout.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment requirements must be verified per format. IQ formats have irregular layouts that may not support aligned wide loads. Need to handle the tail case when the quant data size is not a multiple of the vector width.

optimization_opportunities.description: Extend the reordered (SoA) data layout support from the current 3 formats (Q4_0, Q4_K, Q6_K) to all commonly-used quantization formats, particularly Q8_0, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q4_1, Q2_K, Q3_K, Q5_K. The reordered layout separates quant bytes from scale factors into contiguous regions, enabling coalesced memory access patterns that dramatically improve memory bandwidth utilization.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% throughput improvement for each newly-supported format. The existing Q4_0/Q4_K/Q6_K reordered paths demonstrate the performance benefit. Most LLM models use Q4_K or Q6_K, but Q8_0 and Q5_K are also common.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For each new format: 1) Add reorder_tensor support in quants.hpp/cpp (SoA packing). 2) Implement reorder_mul_mat_vec_<fmt>_q8_1_sycl launcher. 3) Implement the reordered kernel using block_type::get_block_offset(). 4) Wire into the dispatch switch in ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat_vec_q. The existing Q4_0 reorder implementation serves as a template.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Each format has a different block structure, so the reordering logic must be format-specific. Complex formats like Q3_K and Q5_K have multiple sub-fields (qs, qh, scales, d) that all need separate contiguous regions. Must ensure the reorder/dereorder is compatible with other kernel paths that may access the same tensor.

optimization_opportunities.description: Enable GGML_SYCL_F16 build flag to use half-precision arithmetic for scale factor multiplication in vec_dot functions. Several vecdotq.hpp functions (Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1) have conditional FP16 paths under #ifdef GGML_SYCL_F16 that perform dm4 * ds8 in half precision before converting to float.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% for applicable formats. FP16 compute is 2x faster than FP32 on Xe2. However, the scale multiplication is a small fraction of the total compute (dominated by dp4a integer ops), so the overall impact is modest.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON to the CMake build flags. Verify numerical accuracy by running the full test suite with this flag enabled. The GGML_SYCL_F16 paths in vecdotq.hpp (lines ~532, ~614, ~666) are already implemented but disabled by default.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: FP16 has lower precision (~3.3 decimal digits vs ~7 for FP32). For some quantization formats with large scale factors, the reduced precision could introduce noticeable numerical errors. Must validate with accuracy tests, especially for larger models.

optimization_opportunities.description: Clean up DPCT artifacts: replace dpct::dp4a with sycl::vec<int8_t,4> dot product or direct dp4a intrinsic, replace dpct::vectorized_binary with standard SYCL vector operations, remove DPCT_COMPATIBILITY_TEMP guards, replace __dpct_inline__ with standard inline hints.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Minimal direct performance impact. Primarily a code quality and maintainability improvement. May enable better compiler optimization by using standard SYCL constructs.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: 1) dpct::dp4a -> use sycl::dot() on char4 types or keep the dp4a helper but move it out of dpct namespace. 2) dpct::vectorized_binary -> use sycl::vec operations. 3) Remove DPCT_COMPATIBILITY_TEMP checks (always true for Intel). 4) __dpct_inline__ -> inline or SYCL_EXTERNAL. 5) dpct::queue_ptr -> sycl::queue*.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Straightforward refactoring. Each replacement can be tested independently. No algorithmic changes.

kernels.efficiency_notes: MMVQ is inherently memory-bandwidth bound (arithmetic intensity ~0.5 ops/byte for Q4 formats vs the 27 ops/byte compute intensity threshold). The key to performance is maximizing memory bandwidth utilization. The legacy kernel path (17 of 20 formats) uses only 16 work-items per work-group — a severe occupancy limitation on Intel GPUs. The reordered kernels (3 formats) are much better at 256 work-items and SoA layout, but still miss SLM caching of the shared Y vector. The kernel is critical for single-token inference (autoregressive decoding), where the matrix is weights and the vector is the hidden state — this path dominates inference latency.

top_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] — correctness fix and performance baseline
Increase work-group size from 64 to 256+ for better occupancy
Replace dp4a with joint_matrix (XMX) for 4-8x int8 matmul throughput
Increase legacy kernel work-group size from 16 to 256 (adopt reordered kernel pattern for all formats)
Cache Y vector in SLM to eliminate 16x redundant global memory loads across sub-groups
